title: Proxy vs Reverse Proxy (Real-world Examples)

segments.text: Why is Engine Inc. calling reverse proxy? What is the proxy anyways? Let's take a look.
Two common types of proxy, a forward proxy, and reverse proxy. A forward proxy is a server
that sits between a group of client machines and an internet. When those clients make
request to websites on the internet, the forward proxy acts as a middleman, intercept
those requests, and talks to the web servers on behalf of those client machines. Why
would anyone want to do that? Here are a few reasons. One, a forward proxy protects
the client's online identity. By using a forward proxy to connect to a website, the IP
address of the client is hidden from the server. Only the IP address of the proxy is visible,
it would be harder to trace back to the client. Two, a forward proxy can be used
by pass browsing restrictions. Some institutions, governments, schools, and big businesses
use firewalls to restrict access to the internet. By connecting to a forward proxy
outside the firewalls, the client machine can potentially get around these restrictions.
It doesn't always work because the firewalls themselves could block the connections to the
proxy. Three, a forward proxy can be used to block access to certain content. It is not
uncommon for schools and businesses to configure the networks to connect all clients to the
web through the proxy and apply filtering rules to this allows sites like social networks.
It is worth noting that a forward proxy normally requires a client to configure its application
to point to it. For large institutions, they usually apply a technique, contract
and proxy to streamline the process. Its transparent proxy works with layer force
witches to redirect certain types of traffic to the proxy automatically. There is no need to
configure the client machines to use it. It is difficult to bypass its transparent proxy when the
client is on the institution's network. In summary, a forward proxy sits between the client
and the internet and acts on behalf of the client. Now let's take a look at the reverse proxy.
The reverse proxy sits between the internet and the web servers. In the steps to request
from the clients and talk to the web server on behalf of the clients. Why would a
website use a reverse proxy? Here are a few good reasons. One, a reverse proxy could
be used to protect a website. The website's IP addresses are hidden behind the reverse
proxy and are not revealed to the clients. This makes it much harder to target a
doc's attack against a website. Second, a reverse proxy is used for low balancing.
A popular website handling millions of users every day is unlikely to be able to handle
the traffic with a single server. A reverse proxy can balance the large amount of incoming
request by distributing the traffic to a large pool of web servers and effectively
preventing any single one of them from becoming overloaded. Note that this assumes that
the reverse proxy can handle the incoming traffic. Services like Kyle Flair put
reverse proxy servers in hundreds of locations all around the world. This puts
the reverse proxy closer to users and at the same time provides a large amount of
processing capacity. Third, a reverse proxy catches static content. A piece of content
could be cash on the reverse proxy for a period of time. If the same piece of
content is requested again from the reverse proxy, the locally cashed version
could be quickly returned. Fourth, a reverse proxy can handle SSL encryption.
SSL handshake is computationally expensive. A reverse proxy can free up the
origin servers from those expensive operations. Instead of handling SSL for all clients,
a website only needs to handle SSL handshake for a small number of reverse
proxies. Reverse proxies are everywhere. For a modern website, it is not uncommon to have
many layers of reverse proxies. The first layer could be an edge service like
Cloud Flair. The reverse proxies are deployed to hundreds of locations worldwide
closer to the users. The second layer could be an API gateway or low balancer at the
hosting provider. Many cloud providers combine these two layers into a single
grid service. The user would enter the cloud network at the edge close to the user.
And from the edge, the reverse proxy connects over a fast fiber network to the low
balancer, whether request is even in distributed over a cluster of web servers.
